Korean-Style Gochujang Grilled Pork Ribs

This is the grill-country bridge record: country-style pork ribs — those thick, meaty shoulder chops sold as ribs — wearing a gochujang marinade built for low-and-slow-ish grilling rather than the tabletop's speed rounds.

Korean · Medium · Serves 4

Chapter 01 / 20 meat recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: contemporary. This is the grill-country bridge record: country-style pork ribs — those thick, meaty shoulder chops sold as ribs — wearing a gochujang marinade built for low-and-slow-ish grilling rather than the tabletop's speed rounds. It is not a traditional recipe with a lineage to defend; it is the yangnyeom lane's flavor set applied to a cut that loves it, written honestly as a modern build. The technique worth keeping is the two-stage fire: gentle roasting first to render and cook through, then a hot finish to set the glaze.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Marinate long — this cut earns it. Country ribs are thick; the 8–24-hour soak is the difference between glazed meat and spiced meat. Reserve a third of the marinade in a separate container before the ribs go in — that clean portion becomes the finishing glaze.
  • Plan a two-zone fire (or a two-stage oven-and-grill path): one side medium-low for the roast stage, one side hot for the glaze finish. If the tabletop burner is all you have, this record moves to the oven for stage one (160 °C, 25 minutes) and the pan for stage two.
  • Pull the ribs from the fridge 30 minutes ahead.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Stage one — roast gentle. Thick-side down on the cool zone, lid down, turning every 8–10 minutes, 25–30 minutes total. The fat renders slowly and the interior cooks through without the sugars involved yet. No glaze in this stage — glaze on raw heat is the burned-sugar trap. Checkpoint — at stage one's end the meat is firm-poached looking, opaque to the center at a test cut edge (pork's rule: no pink for the cautious table, a faint blush acceptable at exactly 70 °C internal if you measure), and the surface is dry-ish and ready to take glaze.
  2. 02
    Stage two — glaze hot. Move the ribs to the hot zone. Brush the reserved marinade on both faces, turning every 90 seconds, building two or three thin coats — 6–8 minutes total. Each thin coat sets glossy; one thick coat burns. Checkpoint — the surface should go brick-red and tacky-glossy, charred only at the fat edges. If any face blackens, it has had enough fire — back to the cool zone to rest.
  3. 03
    Rest 5 minutes, cut between the bones (or into thick slices for boneless), sesame over, platter. Checkpoint — eating test: the glaze's sweet-heat edge, then rendered-soft shoulder meat that pulls tender under the tooth — this should eat like the best version of backyard ribs that a Korean pantry makes, and the honest note at the table is that it is a modern hybrid, not an old recipe wearing a new one. Chef’s Note — the reserved-glaze habit is the transferable trick: never glaze from the bowl the raw meat marinated in, and never glaze a piece whose sugars have not yet been diluted by rendered juice. Thin coats, many turns — the same law the yangnyeom fried chicken kitchens run at the toss.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Glaze burned before meat doneSingle-stage hot fireTwo-stage: roast first, glaze last
Glaze slid off, paleWet surface or one thick coatDry-ish surface, two or three thin coats
Meat toughCooked fast like a chopStage one at gentle heat, 25–30 minutes
Bitter char tasteBurnt gochujang sugarsCooler hot-zone; fewer minutes per turn

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated ribs keep 24 hours, freeze 1 month. Cooked, 4 days — chop into fried rice or warm into a rice bowl with the last of the reserved glaze.
  • Variations: the marinade doubles on chicken thighs (#M17); a spoon of honey in the final coat for a stickier finish; ssam service with perilla leaf is the Korean table's claim on the platter.
